blindSummary:
This state/province, anchored by the country's capital, is the institutional counterweight to the resolution-belt units. On 6 February 2024 the capital's provincial administrative court repealed the last remaining "against LGBT ideology" document in the country. The capital is the origin point of the progressive response: in February 2019 its mayor signed a 12-point LGBT+ Declaration (security, education, culture, sport, employment; drawn up with LGBT NGOs, including an intervention hostel and school "lighthouse keeper" projects), which provoked the first anti-LGBT municipal resolution in another town (March 2019) as an explicit counter-reaction. The administrative-court campaign, led from the capital by the national Commissioner for Human Rights and carried through the provincial administrative courts and the supreme administrative court, dismantled the resolution network nationally.

The unit's dark stain is historical: in May 2005 the city, under a mayor who later became the country's head of state, banned that year's equality parade, and in 2007 the regional human-rights court ruled the ban violated the convention's assembly, remedy and non-discrimination provisions - a landmark establishing that parade bans require a lawful, non-arbitrary basis. This is 20 years past and has not been repeated.

The unit's record combines a court-led repeal campaign with an active municipal protection programme; the resolution-belt units carry that legacy without any equivalent repeal campaign or declaration infrastructure.
blindSourceSummaries: Encyclopedia overview of the country's "LGBT-free zone" declarations: roughly 100 municipalities plus five first-level units (about a third of the country) adopted "against LGBT ideology" resolutions or family-rights charters by 2020; unenforceable but stigmatising, and widely reported as a direct reaction to the capital's February 2019 declaration. On 6 February 2024 the capital's provincial administrative court repealed the last such document in the country, and by 24 April 2025 all anti-LGBT resolutions and charters had been withdrawn or invalidated by court order.

City-network blog account of how the capital's 12-point LGBT+ Declaration was made (March 2019): drafted with local associations (an LGBT campaigner and their advocacy group), promising measures in security, education, culture, sport, administration and employment - including shelter for teenagers rejected by families and anti-discrimination and sex education in schools; it sparked backlash from the then right-wing national government and the dominant church. The capital's near-two million residents include an estimated 200,000 LGBT+ people.

Encyclopedia case summary of a 2007 regional human-rights court judgment: the pre-publication ban of the 2005 capital equality parade by the city's chief executive (later the country's head of state) violated the convention's freedom-of-assembly, effective-remedy and non-discrimination provisions; a landmark establishing that parade bans require a lawful, non-arbitrary basis.

Legal explainer of the declaration-to-repeal arc (2019-2025): the national human-rights ombudsman litigated from December 2019; provincial administrative courts held the resolutions violated the constitutional equal-treatment guarantee, upheld by the supreme administrative court; the supranational bloc tied cohesion funding to charter compliance (76.5bn in bloc currency suspended, ~136bn frozen overall), driving council withdrawals; the last remaining zone was abolished in May 2025. The resolutions were "legally meaningless" but, per a 2025 statement by the continent-wide council's human-rights commissioner, "directly impact the lives of LGBTI people".
blindTangential: The 2019-2025 resolution fight and the bloc funding conditionality concerned LGBT+ rights broadly (family-charters and sex-curriculum language rather than gender-expression enforcement) - their force for trans visitors is the institutional signal they carried.
blindLocalsOnly: The capital declaration's operational measures - the intervention hostel for rejected teenagers and the school support projects - serve residents; a visitor uses none of them but reads the institutional climate they created.
